notes.meaning: Fourteen years after his first visit, Paul traveled back to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus. Barnabas was a trusted Jewish Christian leader, while Titus was a Greek convert. Paul shared this story to show that he worked in full agreement with the Jerusalem apostles, even though he did not receive his authority from them.

Paul went to Jerusalem because God directed him through a revelation, not because church leaders summoned him. He explained the gospel message he preached among the Gentiles, speaking privately with the most respected leaders. He wanted to make sure they were in full agreement so that false rumors would not divide the church or undo his work.

Even though Titus was an uncircumcised Greek, the apostles in Jerusalem did not force him to be circumcised. Circumcision was the physical sign of the Jewish law of Moses. By welcoming Titus as a brother, the leaders confirmed that non-Jewish believers do not need to follow Jewish rituals to belong to God's family.

Some false teachers had slipped into the church meetings to spy on the freedom believers have in Jesus. They wanted to force Christians back into the slavery of relying on ceremonies for salvation. Paul and his team refused to give in to their demands for even a moment, so that the pure truth of the gospel would be preserved for all believers.

The widely respected leaders in Jerusalem did not add anything new to Paul's message. Paul respected their position, but he remembered that God does not play favorites or judge by human titles. God had already given Paul the complete message of salvation directly through Christ.

The apostles recognized that God gave Paul the mission of preaching to the Gentiles, just as He gave Peter the mission to reach the Jews. The same Lord worked with mighty spiritual power in both men to change lives. Although their mission fields were different, they shared the very same gospel.

James, Peter, and John, who were seen as pillars of the church, clearly saw the grace of God on Paul's ministry. They shook hands with Paul and Barnabas as equal partners in Christ's work. They agreed that Paul and Barnabas would go to the Gentiles, while the Jerusalem leaders focused on reaching the Jewish people.

The Jerusalem leaders made only one request: that Paul and Barnabas remember to care for the poor believers in Judea. Paul was already eager to help them, knowing that practical love unites Christians across cultural lines. Caring for those in need is an essential fruit of living out the gospel.

Later, when Peter visited the church in Antioch, Paul had to oppose him face to face. Peter had acted in a way that was clearly wrong and harmful to the church. Paul corrected him publicly because Peter's public actions were confusing believers and threatening the truth of the gospel.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching explains that Peter's fault was in his personal conduct and pastoral judgment, not in defining church dogma. A pope's gift of infallibility applies only when he solemnly defines a matter of faith or morals for the whole church, not to his daily private actions.

notes.meaning: At first, Peter freely shared meals with Gentile Christians, knowing God accepts them without the law of Moses. But when visitors from Jerusalem arrived, Peter pulled away and refused to eat with Gentiles because he feared the criticism of the strict Jewish group. His sudden retreat treated Gentile believers as though they were unclean.

The other Jewish believers in Antioch followed Peter's bad example and acted dishonestly along with him. Even Barnabas, Paul's close missionary partner, was swept up in this peer pressure. Their withdrawal made it seem as though Gentile believers were second-class citizens in God's household.

Paul noticed that their steps were crooked and did not line up with the truth of the good news. He confronted Peter in front of everyone for his double standard. Since Peter was a Jew who had been living freely like a Gentile, he had no right to force Gentile believers to live by Jewish customs.

Paul reminded Peter that both of them were born Jews and not Gentile outsiders raised without God's law. Even with their heritage and spiritual privileges, their Jewish background could not save them. Heritage and good upbringing do not give anyone a special claim on God's favor.

differ.view: Some Presbyterians emphasize that justification means God treats the believer as if he had never sinned on the ground of Christ's merits, rather than a literal transfer of moral character.

notes.meaning: A person is justified—declared right with God—only through faith in Jesus Christ, and never by doing works required by the law. Even Jewish believers had to place their faith in Jesus because keeping commandments cannot make anyone right before God. Salvation is received as a free gift by trusting in Christ alone.

differ.view: Some Presbyterians emphasize that justification means God treats the believer as if he had never sinned on the ground of Christ's merits, rather than a literal transfer of moral character.

notes.meaning: Opponents claimed that turning away from the law to trust Christ alone makes people careless sinners. Paul strongly rejected this idea, asking if Christ promotes sin by setting believers free from ritual rules. Trusting Jesus for righteousness reveals our real need for Him, but it never makes Christ a servant of sin.

A person becomes a real lawbreaker by rebuilding the legal system of rules they had already torn down. Going back to rule-keeping to earn salvation implies that trusting Christ was a mistake. The fault lies entirely with the person who turns back, not with the gospel of grace.

The law itself showed Paul that he was a helpless sinner and could never save himself, driving him to Christ. By dying with Christ, he died to the law's power to condemn him. Being freed from the legal covenant allowed him to begin living a brand-new life entirely for God.

Believers share in the death of Jesus, so their old life dominated by sin has been crucified with Him. The Christian no longer lives alone, because Christ lives within through His Spirit. Daily life in this body is now lived by faith in the Son of God, who showed His love by giving His life on the cross.

differ.view: Lutherans emphasize that faith joins the believer so completely to Christ that sin, death, and the devil are crucified, bringing peace to a terrified conscience apart from good works.

notes.meaning: Paul refused to reject or make void the grace of God by trying to earn salvation through human effort. If people could become right with God by obeying the law, then Christ died for no purpose at all. Relying on Christ's sacrifice honors God's wonderful, unearned gift of eternal life.
